rv.q: No matter what mood you’re in when you arrive at the St. James Theatre, you’ll go home grinning with delight.
In the hands of Kline and a vividly intelligent supporting cast, it’s a great and frank and still modern comedy.
This contradiction has found a blissful home as Garry Essendine, the reluctantly aging, casually devastating matinee idol in 'Present Laughter.'
Kline relishes the comic challenge in this snazzy production directed by Moritz von Stuelpnagel.
Kline enlivens each moment with palpable zest and impeccable style, arrogant brio shading into middle-aged insecurity with a twitch of his perfectly trimmed mustache.

That arch knowingness in the writing finds sublime echoes in Kline’s performance, that of a consummate theater creature returning to his natural domain with obvious relish, playing an actor who is always performing, on and off the stage.
Mr. Kline is so compulsively watchable, so utterly and consummately in control of the proceedings that we simply surrender to an actor at the top of his game.

Moritz von Stuelpnagel's revival is fleet, funny, deliciously cast and over the top when it should be – and occasionally when it needn't be, sweating just a bit too hard to earn the audience's whoops of pleasure.
Mr. Kline, I am delighted to report, fully delivers on the promise of that entrance, building a paradoxically natural performance as a man for whom the histrionic gesture is a conditioned reflex.
Kline and company know what they're doing, making it a nightcap you won't want to turn down.
Garry is a hollow character, but Kline puts him together with care and shrewdness.
The result is that laughter is only intermittently present. It feels lugubrious and weighty rather effortless.
However, it is Kline who anchors the production, in a performance of exceptional clarity that wears the heavy mantle of light comedy with ease.
He's a brilliant comedian in a leading man's body, and he fits the role like a Savile Row suit.
A brilliantly fine-tuned comedy of style and substance...
It makes for an irresistible cocktail of a show.
And Kline's nimble hands deserve their own applause from theatergoers at the St. James.
The moments of Kline and Burton together represent the production's peak of civilized high comedy.
Kline — whose movie career includes turns as both Cole Porter and Errol Flynn — takes to it like, well, a pig to slop.
Blessedly, Noel Coward knew that and Kevin Kline really gets it.
The result although amusing is uneven with Kline standing out as the glorious spirit of the evening.
The reason to go to the St. James Theater is to escape from reality for a few hours and enjoy a significantly stylish but thematically insignificant farce
Something in the writing of Present Laughter never raises the stakes to the level of gasping hilarity that true farce can elicit.
At other times, it is veddy British, proper, and absolutely terrific — especially when Kevin Kline and Kate Burton are on stage, which, fortunately, is most of the time.
He just never leaves us with the sense things are spinning dangerously out of control.
This revival is a perfectly pleasant evening, but it's also a perfectly safe one.
There seems to have been no point in reviving the play other than to provide Kline with a star vehicle.
But that present, at least as offered at the St. James, seems to have passed.
The stage is a boiling pot of combustible energy.
With Kevin Kline stepping in to lead the company, Present Laughter is a pièce de résistance this theater season.
Kevin Kline is the best Essendine that I’ve seen.
Kevin Kline is a national treasure, and we're luck he's on Broadway, giving us the present of laughter.
This makes for a very textured Present Laughter.
And in fact, nothing goes “too far” in this perfectly calibrated, splendid, crazy, high-spirited, yes, farce.
For the life of me, I cannot see why, and Present Laughter serves as a delightful rebuke to this trend, proving that there’s always more room for madcap farce on the Great White Way.

If the posh, harried life of a wealthy actor or the cascading blunders of a flailing theatre troupe don't sound like much to sink your teeth into, rest assured it's all in the delivery — and worth the payoff of escape.

Present Laughter...is a wonderful reminder of what mid-20th-century Broadway audiences attended back in the day...as a vehicle for an actor like Kevin Kline, it's worth every penny of your Broadway dollars.

tn.cat: Best Costume Design of a Play

aw.sub: Won Best Actor in a Play

cn.t: Critics praise Kevin Kline's masterful return to Broadway after a decade, calling his performance in this Coward revival impeccable and perfectly matched to the role, though some find the 1939 comedy itself dated and the production uneven.

vs.sum: The St. James Theatre offers good sightlines for most seats, though the lack of a solid rake can be an issue if someone tall sits in front of you. The sound quality is generally good, but the tight legroom can be uncomfortable for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic and grand interior, while facilities are average with standard amenities.

acc.note: No steps from sidewalk to Orchestra. No elevator. Mezzanine up 29 steps, Balcony up 76 steps.
